This repo is a Flask fork called `tessel`. The code is all in `src/tessel/views.py`, and the names differ from Flask's.

**Turning the class into a view function**
- `View.to_view_func(cls, name, *class_args, **class_kwargs)` is a classmethod. It builds an inner `view(**kwargs)` closure.
- If `init_every_request` is true, the closure creates a new instance of the class on each request. Otherwise it creates one instance up front and reuses it.
- The closure then calls `active_app.ensure_sync(self.run_view)(**kwargs)`.
- Any `decorators` on the class are applied to the closure.
- The closure gets `view_class`, `methods` and `provide_automatic_options` attributes copied from the class. Route registration (`attach_route_rule(..., view_func=...)`) reads these.

**Routing HTTP methods to `get()` and `post()`**
- Your class needs to subclass `VerbView`, which extends `View`.
- `VerbView.__init_subclass__` runs when the subclass is defined. For each name in `http_method_funcs` (`get`, `post`, `put`, and so on) that the class has, it adds the uppercase name to `cls.methods`. It also merges in `methods` from base classes. This is how the route learns which HTTP methods to accept.
- `VerbView.run_view(**kwargs)` is what the closure calls on each request. It does `getattr(self, request.method.lower())`, so a POST goes to `post()`. A HEAD request with no `head` method falls back to `get`. It asserts if there is no handler. It calls the handler through `active_app.ensure_sync(meth)(**kwargs)`, which wraps async handlers so they can run.
